history.heading: Plantation islands
paragraphs: São Tomé and Príncipe, two volcanic islands in the Gulf of Guinea off Central Africa, were uninhabited when Portuguese navigators arrived around 1470. Portugal settled them with convicts, Jewish children deported from Portugal and enslaved Africans, and the islands became one of the first plantation economies, growing sugar, and a hub of the slave trade.

In the 19th century, coffee and especially cocoa plantations (roças) made the islands the world's largest cocoa producer around 1908, using contract labourers from Angola, Mozambique and Cape Verde in conditions close to slavery. In the 1953 Batepá massacre, Portuguese authorities killed hundreds of local Creoles.

history.heading: Independence
paragraphs: São Tomé and Príncipe became independent on 12 July 1975 under a one-party socialist government. Multiparty democracy was introduced in 1990–91, and the country has had several peaceful changes of power, though also some coup attempts.

culture.heading: Creole culture
paragraphs: Portuguese is official, and Creole languages such as Forro are spoken. Most people are Catholic. Traditional theatre such as Tchiloli, based on a Portuguese medieval story, and the Danço-Congo are distinctive. Calulu, a fish or meat stew with vegetables, is the national dish.

politics.heading: Semi-presidential republic
paragraphs: São Tomé and Príncipe is a semi-presidential democracy with a directly elected president and a prime minister. Príncipe has its own autonomous regional government. Tensions between the president and the government have sometimes caused crises.

economy.heading: Cocoa and tourism
paragraphs: Cocoa remains the main export, now often organic and high quality. Tourism, built on rainforests, beaches and biodiversity, is growing. The country depends heavily on foreign aid and imports most of its food and fuel. Offshore oil exploration has not yet led to production. The currency is the dobra, pegged to the euro.
